Flood & climate — research notes and sources

What is real and what is assumed. Sea level, storm-tide and rainfall numbers below come from the cited sources. Ground elevation does not: your model's terrain is flat, so the simulation uses a synthetic elevation (1.6 m at the shoreline, rising about 1.05 m per 100 real metres inland, capped at 16 m, in m NAVD88). It is tuned so that a Sandy-level storm floods roughly a quarter of the mapped land and a 2050s 100-year surge about a third, comparable to the city's own 37% figure, but that is calibration, not validation. Replace it with NYC LiDAR for real results. Treat everything here as a design hypothesis, not a prediction.

How the simulation works

  • Water level = storm-tide elevation at the Battery (today's climate) + sea level rise for the chosen year and scenario (minus the ~0.05 m already in today's figures).
  • Coastal flooding spreads inland only from connected water: a cell floods when the water level is above its elevation and a neighbour is flooded (so low ground behind higher ground stays dry).
  • Barrier raises a 60 m shoreline band to the chosen crest height. If the water is higher than the crest it overtops and floods as if there were no wall (a conservative simplification: no volume limit, no pumping).
  • Rain ponding = rainfall above the sewer capacity (1.75 in/hr, one hour) pooling more in low ground. The weighting by elevation is my own illustration, not a drainage model.
  • Land and water come from rasterised roads, buildings and parks of the earlier model (checked against satellite imagery); piers and bridges are treated as water. Horizontal units are Web-Mercator metres, which overstate real distances by about 1.32× at this latitude, so areas and distances in the readouts are corrected by 0.759. Building heights are true metres (One WTC: 541 m). Model: “Manhattan OSM Complete Model” by MENUDQ2, CC BY 4.0, from OpenStreetMap data, cropped and re-scaled.
  • Future rain: the rain slider is multiplied by 1.11 in the 2050s and 1.13 in the 2080s, using the high end of NPCC's projected rise in annual precipitation as a floor. Hourly extremes may grow faster; that is not modelled.
  • Flood recurrence asks how often a Sandy-level water level (3.44 m) is exceeded once sea level has risen, shifting today's return-period curve by the sea level rise. Storm frequency and intensity are held constant.

Sea level rise (NPCC4, 2024)

  • Middle-range projections for NYC (relative to 1995–2014): 7–11 in by the 2030s, 14–19 in (0.36–0.48 m) by the 2050s and 25–39 in (0.64–0.99 m) by the 2080s. NPCC4 summary · NPCC4 paper (Ann. NY Acad. Sci.)
  • Paths in the simulator: Low, High and Very high are the NPCC4 (2024) 25th, 75th and 90th percentiles for the NYC region, relative to 1995–2014: 18/28/33 cm (2030s), 36/48/58 cm (2050s), 64/99/114 cm (2080s) and 76/127/165 cm (2100). NPCC4 (2024)
  • New York State's assessment gives 14–19 in by the 2050s and 30–50 in (0.76–1.27 m) by 2100 at the Battery, used for the low/high 2100 values. NYS Climate Impacts Assessment
  • The earlier high-end design path (about 0.76 m by the 2050s, 1.5 m by the 2080s, 1.9 m by 2100, relative to 2000–04) is kept for comparison. Gornitz et al. · NPCC4 Years between anchors are linearly interpolated.
  • Open data: NYC climate projections dataset.

Tides, sun and wind

  • Tide datums at the Battery (NOAA 8518750, 1983–2001 epoch): MHHW 1.541 m, MHW 1.443 m, MSL 0.783 m above MLLW, and NAVD88 0.846 m above MLLW. Sandy's highest total water level was 4.28 m above MLLW (about 3.43 m NAVD88), total water, not pure surge. NOAA benchmarks
  • City study (2019): 37% of Lower Manhattan properties exposed to a 100-year surge in the 2050s and 47% in 2100; about 20% of streets with daily tidal flooding in 2100; groundwater rise could reach over 450 buildings and 17 miles of streets with utilities. LMCR study
  • Sun: solar position from the standard NOAA equations for the Battery, with New York clock time. Sun-hours ray-march the modelled building heights over a 12 m grid at half-hour steps; ground elevation and trees are ignored.
  • Wind: speed and direction are your inputs (the research table has no wind data). Speed grows with height by a power law with exponent 0.30. The streaks are illustrative, not a flow simulation. Typical prevailing directions (north-west in winter, south-west in summer) are general knowledge, not from the research table.
  • Climate frequencies (NPCC4, 25th–75th percentile): days at or above 90°F rise from about 17 (1981–2010) to 38–62 in the 2050s and 46–85 in the 2080s; heat waves from 2 to 5–8 and 6–9 a year; days with 2 in of rain in 24 h from 3 to 4–5 and 4–6.

Tidal ("sunny day") flooding

  • The Battery has about 10 high-tide floods a year now; that could reach 60–85 days a year by the 2040s. City Limits on NYSERDA · Habitat
  • The city's FiDi–Seaport plan expects tidal flooding to become monthly by the 2050s and daily by the 2080s. master plan ch. 4 · SPCR

Storm tides at the Battery

  • Return-period still-water elevations used (ft NAVD88 → m): 10-yr 6.9 → 2.10, 50-yr 9.9 → 3.02, 100-yr 11.4 → 3.47, 500-yr 14.9 → 4.54; mean higher high water about 2.3 ft → 0.69 m. They come from a conference slide on NOAA/FEMA values, so check against FEMA's current study before relying on them. Cornell NRCC slide
  • Sandy's record: 11.3 ft NAVD88 at the Battery (about 3.44 m), beating Donna's 7.2 ft in 1960. NYC NPCC report Another study estimates a much longer return period for Sandy (about 1,570 years), so return-period estimates differ. UMass-hosted paper
  • Sandy: peak 13.88 ft above MLLW with a 9.23 ft surge. Climate Central The weather service reported 3–5 ft of inundation along the West Side Highway, Battery Park and FDR Drive, reaching several blocks inland. NWS
  • Simulated storm frequency changes in one modelling study were minimal for NYC; the main change is the higher sea level the surge rides on. PNAS-linked study

Extreme rain

  • The sewer system is designed for about 1.75 in/hr; Ida (Sept 2021) dropped 3.15 in in an hour in Central Park, the wettest hour on record then, after Henri's 1.94 in. Scientific American · Bloomberg
  • FEMA found the drainage in much of the city handles only about 1.5 in/hr. Scientific American
  • The city's stormwater flood maps use 1.77 in/hr (limited), 2.13 in/hr (moderate, paired with +0.76 m for 2050) and 3.66 in/hr (extreme, paired with +1.46 m for 2080). The map classes depths of 4–12 in (10–30 cm) as nuisance flooding and over 12 in as deep flooding, and ignores ponds under 0.25 acre. NYC Stormwater Flood Maps · NYC Hazard Mitigation Plan
  • Landfilled historic streams and wetlands are now low, flood-exposed ground. NPCC4 flooding brief

Heat (state and NPCC projections)

  • Days above 95°F: about 4 a year historically, 14–32 by mid-century and 17–54 by the end of the century. NYS Climate Impacts Assessment

Heat and precipitation (NPCC 2015 projections)

  • Days at or above 90°F in Central Park: 18 today, up to 46 by the 2050s and up to 76 by the 2080s (high end). Global Citizen · Inside Climate News
  • Annual precipitation +4–11% by the 2050s and +5–13% by the 2080s; heat-wave frequency projected to triple by the 2080s. NPCC 2015 (NYC) NPCC4 (2024) updated these projections; the 2015 numbers are shown as context only.

Protection projects and schedule

  • Anticipated completion: Brooklyn Bridge–Montgomery 2026, South Battery Park City 2026, The Battery 2027, Seaport 2029, North-West Battery Park City 2030; East Side Coastal Resiliency 2027. NYC LMCR · LMCR quarterly, Mar 2026 · City & State
  • The FiDi–Seaport stretch is the last link and is still in design, so the simulator leaves it unprotected. City Limits
  • The city says over $2.7 billion has been committed. nyc.gov/lmcr Zone boundaries in the simulator are my approximations from the satellite image.
  • A 2018 city briefing draft cited 100-year surges of 9–16 ft by 2100. LMCR briefing (draft)

City benchmarks (for comparison with the simulator)

  • By the 2050s, with about 30 in of sea level rise, 37% of properties in Lower Manhattan are at risk from storm surge. NYC Mayor's Office
  • By 2100, with over 6 ft of rise, almost 50% of properties are at risk from storm surge and 20% of streets face daily tidal inundation. LMCR study
  • Groundwater rise is projected to endanger 7% of buildings and 39% of streets with underground utilities (not simulated here). NYC Mayor's Office
  • Seaport Coastal Resilience design flood elevation: 11 ft NAVD88 (3.35 m); by 2100 daily high tides could reach up to three blocks inland at Pearl Street. SPCR, Oct 2024
  • The FiDi–Seaport plan is the last link and still in design; most other projects should finish by 2031. City Limits

Made land and 1609 ecology

  • Original eastern shoreline ≈ Pearl Street; landfill reached Water Street by about 1730, Front Street by 1780 and South Street by 1800. Skyscraper Museum Fill is 20–35 ft deep in places. Archaeology
  • Mannahatta/Welikia found over 55 ecological communities in 1609. Welikia overview
  • Map sources: NYPL 1900 Manhattan, Viele 1865.
